But if I’m traveling or in a hurry, I’ll turn to them—and rarely without this shave gel from GilletteLabs. The rapid foaming is as advertised, thickening in seconds for quick application.

It gives that fresh feeling once it hits your face before the razor even touches your skin. While it’s listed as having a cedar wood and orange peel scent, I rarely catch too much of it. But I prefer that, as I’d rather rely on my cologne for fragrance.

I implore you to use a shave oil in addition to a cream to minimize irritation as much as possible; however, if you really don’t have the time or desire to, use this. Atwater’s shaving cream is designed to pull double duty, preparing the skin before the razor touches it and protecting it throughout the shave. As a pre-shave, its blend of hydrating oils helps soften stubble and create a smooth, conditioned surface.

During shaving, ingredients like vitamin B5, vitamin C, argan oil, and coconut oil work together to cushion the blade, reduce friction, and keep the skin nourished. This combination leaves my skin feeling as calm and moisturized as it’ll get without using a pre-shave oil. Plus, it’s completely unscented, so it’s safe for even the most sensitive skin.

Dr. Squatch’s shave butter feels more like a creamy lotion than shaving cream, allowing the razor to glide smoothly across the skin while it also moisturizes. Despite how that sounds, it never clogs up my blade—even when I use a safety razor. The trio of natural hero ingredients, shea butter, murumuru butter, and macadamia oil, is rich in vitamins and fatty acids that deeply hydrate, soften, and smooth the skin.

Together, they create a nourishing barrier that locks in moisture and helps reduce irritation for a more comfortable, soothing shave. The lotion-like texture takes a couple of shaves to get used to if you’ve traditionally used thicker shave creams or foams, but the feel of your skin during and after is immediately satisfying.

Shaving cream is often used as a catch-all term for several products that prep and protect your skin while you shave. There are three main types, and the right one depends on your razor, your skin type, and your personal preference.

If your shave is only as good as the cream you use, then the cream is only as good as its ingredients. Shaving creams often include soothing ingredients like aloe vera, which calms irritation and helps the skin stay hydrated before and after shaving. Shea butter is another popular one, as it provides rich moisture that softens hair and improves razor glide, reducing friction during the shave.

Many formulas also contain vitamin E, an antioxidant that nourishes the skin and supports repair after shaving. Then there is a slew of natural oils and other vitamins to keep an eye on, like vitamin B5, vitamin C, argan oil, and coconut oil that hydrate, soothe, and prevent post-shave irritation.

How often do you shave? That’s the most important question to ask yourself when considering the size of your cream. A larger tube offers better value and lasts longer, especially for daily shavers. Smaller sizes, on the other hand, are ideal for travel or testing a new formula before committing. You’ll also want to consider what you shave.

I rock a beard most of the time, so I only shave for touch-ups on my neck and cheeks. Plus, I rarely shave body hair and stick to trimming. Because of this, I can often get away with a smaller tube. But if you’re clean-cut or shave large parts of your body, you’ll want to look to larger options.

#4981. Tesla (TSLA) releases Q3 2026 financial results: margins rebound, profit still falls

Tesla (TSLA) released its financial results and shareholders’ letter for the third quarter (Q3) 2026 after market close today. We’re updating this post with all the details from the financial results, shareholders’ letter, and the conference call later tonight.

The earnings call with management is scheduled for 5:30 p.m. ET.

Wall Street came into the report expecting a flat quarter. The FactSet consensus, as displayed on Estimize, called for $28.06 billion in revenue, essentially unchanged from the $28.1 billion Tesla posted in Q3 2025 and a bit below the $28.24 billion it reported last quarter.

Profit expectations were lower. Analysts were looking for non-GAAP earnings of $0.45 per share, down 10% from $0.50 a year ago. The Estimize crowd was slightly more bullish at $28.36 billion and $0.48.

We already had the volume numbers. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in Q3, down 2.1% year-over-year but well ahead of the 461,974 consensus, while producing only 464,391. It also deployed 13.7 GWh of energy storage, up from 12.5 GWh a year ago but short of the roughly 15.9 GWh analysts expected. For the full setup, see our Q3 2026 earnings preview.

So the question was never volume. It was whether Tesla could stop the profit slide after Q2, when operating margin fell to 1.4% and EPS missed the consensus by 20 cents.

After the market closed today, Tesla released its financial results for the third quarter and reported $28.05 billion in revenue, flat from a year ago and in line with the $28.06 billion Wall Street expected. Non-GAAP earnings came in at $0.48 per share, beating the $0.45 consensus but down 4% from $0.50 a year ago.

It’s a better quarter than Q2, but the trend hasn’t changed. Margins recovered, with auto gross margin excluding credits back above 18%, yet operating income still fell 56% year-over-year as spending on AI and Optimus grew faster than gross profit. On a GAAP basis, net income dropped 43% to $787 million, or $0.22 per share.

Total gross margin was 19.6%, up 160 basis points from 18.0% a year ago and well above the 16.8% Tesla posted in Q2. Operating income fell 56% to $718 million, for an operating margin of 2.6%, compared with 5.8% a year ago and 1.4% last quarter.

Operating expenses came in at $4.78 billion, up 39% year-over-year. Research and development alone jumped 69% to $2.76 billion as Tesla spends on what it now calls “Super Intelligence” (SI), Optimus, and the Cybercab. Stock-based compensation, which includes the 2025 CEO pay package, hit $1.17 billion, up from $663 million a year ago.

Capital spending was $4.73 billion, more than double the $2.25 billion of a year ago, and free cash flow came in at $1.53 billion, compared with $3.99 billion a year ago and negative $1.09 billion in Q2. Tesla ended the quarter with $45.4 billion in cash and investments. GAAP net income included a $288 million unrealized gain on Tesla’s bitcoin holdings, partly offset by a $142 million unrealized loss on its SpaceX equity investment.

That puts Tesla’s capex at $13.01 billion through the first nine months of 2026, only about half of the “more than $25 billion” management guided for the year. To hit that number, Tesla would need to spend roughly $12 billion in Q4 alone, more than double its biggest quarter so far. The Q3 letter doesn’t update the guidance, and capex actually fell sequentially from $5.79 billion in Q2. So either Q4 spending explodes, or the 2026 plan is quietly slipping into 2027. The lower spending also flatters this quarter’s positive free cash flow.

The number we watch first is automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits, now that the credit market has mostly dried up. It came in at 18.1% this quarter, up from 16.3% in Q2 and 15.4% a year ago, though still below the 19.2% of Q1, when Tesla got help from warranty and tariff one-time benefits. Tesla credits a better regional and product mix and more FSD subscription revenue, partly offset by lower average selling prices.

Regulatory credits brought in just $113 million, down 73% from $417 million a year ago and below the $146 million in Q2. That line isn’t coming back now that automakers no longer pay federal fuel-economy penalties.

Energy was the weak spot on revenue. Energy generation and storage revenue fell 16% to $2.88 billion, which Tesla partly blames on tariff-related customer refunds, even though deployments rose 10% to 13.7 GWh. The segment’s gross margin jumped to 33% from 20% in Q2, but energy gross profit still slipped to $954 million from $1.07 billion a year ago.

Services and other was the bright spot. Revenue grew 33% to $4.61 billion, and Tesla says gross profit hit a record $734 million on charging, insurance and parts sales.

Tesla says “battery availability continued to be the limiting factor in increasing auto volumes in the quarter,” and that it ended Q3 with “the largest backlog for our passenger vehicles in four years.”

That’s a new explanation for flat sales. Deliveries were still down 2% year-over-year, “other models” (Cybertruck, Semi, Model S and X) fell 48%, and Tesla delivered 22,141 more cars than it built, bringing inventory down to 11 days of supply from 15 in Q2. But average selling prices fell again, which isn’t usually what a supply-constrained automaker does.

On autonomy, Tesla says active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74 million, up 67%, though that count includes upfront purchases, as defined in Musk’s 2025 pay package. Its Robotaxi service reached nearly 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles by the end of the quarter, a month after Cybercab joined the Austin fleet.

I am still waiting for the 50% YOY growth rate that Musk touted a few years ago to justify the TSLA valuation. Then I reminded myself that TSLA is just the largest MEME stock in the market day.

Tesla’s full Q3 2026 shareholder deck is available on the company’s investor relations site, and management will discuss the results on the earnings call at 5:30 p.m. ET.

This is a developing story. We’ll add the most important updates from Tesla’s shareholder letter and earnings call here as they come.

#4980. Erin and Sara Foster Reveal the Rule That Keeps Their Business—and Sisterhood—Working

The Nobody Wants This producers stop by the latest episode of The Huddle.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Whether you’ve binged all three seasons of the Netflix comedy Nobody Wants This, presided over a board meeting in your chicest Favorite Daughter blazer, or nodded along to a cringey dating anecdote while listening to The World’s First Podcast, you are no doubt familiar with the work of multi-hyphenate sisters Erin and Sara Foster.

Raised in Los Angeles (dad is famous record producer David Foster), the sisters first gained notoriety with their VH1 mockumentary series, Barely Famous, in 2015. Since then, they’ve gone on to launch several successful businesses, including their clothing line and a production company, Fatigue Sisters Productions. (They even recently served as guest sharks on ABC’s Shark Tank.)

With the season 3 premiere of Nobody Wants This (based on Erin’s own experience of dating and marrying a Jewish man and later converting to Judaism), the dynamic duo stopped by the Women’s Health podcast The Huddle to chat with editors Abby Cuffey and Jacqueline Andriakos about doing business together, setting boundaries, and raising kids.

Erin and Sara launched their clothing line, Favorite Daughter, in late 2020 to fill gaps in their own closets. But as the company has grown and evolved over time, they’ve learned to put their customers at the heart of everything they do. It’s also forced the sisters to staff up with people who are willing to share their true opinions, rather than simply being yes-men or yes-women.

“That's something that is really challenging when you have a talent-focused brand,” Erin says. “It's taken a very long time for us to convince the people who work for us to be honest with us. That’s how people become monsters—no one's telling them the truth.”

“I always say, too, this is a democracy,” Sara adds. “This only works if everyone feels heard. This only works if you're allowed to do the thing that you're hired to do.”

Having a valued third or even fourth opinion also comes in handy when the two can’t see eye-to-eye, which happened often when the brand first launched.

“We’re in a good place today, but we would have blow-up screaming fights in fittings for many years at Favorite Daughter,” Erin says. “It’s tricky for us, because we do not have differentiated, carved-out roles. We have the exact same role, so if we disagree, it's really challenging to find the happy medium.”

In 2021, the sisters’ working relationship expanded further when they launched their podcast The World's First Podcast with Erin & Sara Foster. While the duo aren’t shy about diving into personal topics—be it romantic relationships or raising children—they have set certain boundaries to ensure their friends and family don’t end up embarrassed or as headline fodder.

“I have an idea of where [my husband’s] boundaries are,” Erin says. “He's not really into me talking about exes or other relationships.”

Sara, on the other hand, learned the hard way where one of her daughter’s boundaries lie when she revealed her juvenile arthritis diagnosis—in the hopes of helping other parents—and it was picked up by multiple outlets.

“It never occurred to me that that could happen,” Sara says. “My daughter was like, ‘I do not appreciate that.’ I was like, ‘Oh god, I'm so sorry.’”

Given that they have creative control over the podcast’s content, Erin and Sara do occasionally edit out portions that they think could be taken out of context with the TikTok-ification of media nowadays. “We try to err on the side of keeping things in, but then there's some times that you get a little ahead of yourself,” Erin says.

Speaking of raising daughters, Sara’s got even more wisdom to share on parenting—specifically about telling your kids the harsh truths about yourself.

“Being a mother is just such a exercise in getting humbled,” she says. “My instinct was always like, don't reveal yourself too much. Don't let them see your flaws. Don't tell them about all the times you f---ed up as a teenager yourself. But that's the opposite. You're really supposed to. Maybe some people disagree with this, but as they get older, you’re supposed to reveal mistakes you made, things that you wish you did differently... That has changed the dynamic with me and my older daughter—being honest with her about things that I wish I had done differently.”

Erin agrees: “I think it's probably better for your children to grow up knowing that you are a complicated, flawed person, and then you don't have to fall off a pedestal for them.”

To hear more from the sisters about how they find the creativity to create, their stance on kids and social media, and why they’re obsessed with a certain protein powder, click play on the latest episode of The Huddle above!

#4975. Tesla blames battery supply for flat sales, but its prices keep falling

Tesla says battery supply, not demand, is what’s holding back its car sales. In its Q3 2026 shareholder letter, the automaker wrote that “battery availability continued to be the limiting factor in increasing auto volumes in the quarter.”

It also claims it ended Q3 with “the largest backlog for our passenger vehicles in four years.” But the numbers in the same letter don’t line up with a company that has more buyers than cars.

The battery line has been building for a while. In Q2, Tesla called battery pack capacity “the main limiting factor to near-term vehicle production volume increase.” Now it says batteries limited what it could sell during the quarter itself.

Tesla didn’t put a number on the backlog. It did list record deliveries in Canada, Australia, Japan and Taiwan, and record production at Gigafactory Berlin. Elsewhere in the Q3 2026 financial results, Tesla says it is focused on “increasing production across our factories” because of “strong demand.”

Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in Q3, down 2% from 497,099 a year ago. Model 3 and Model Y were down 1%. “Other models,” which covers Cybertruck, Semi and what’s left of Model S and X, fell 48% to 8,295 units.

It built 464,391 vehicles, so it delivered 22,141 more than it produced. That’s the second quarter in a row Tesla has worked down inventory, after building about 50,000 more cars than it sold in Q1. Global inventory fell to 11 days of supply, from 27 days in Q1 and 15 in Q2.

Model 3 and Model Y production ran at about 1.83 million units annualized. Tesla lists more than 2.25 million units of installed capacity for those two models across Fremont, Shanghai, Berlin and Texas. So the factories ran at roughly 81%.

And here’s the part that doesn’t fit. In its list of reasons revenue didn’t grow, Tesla cited “lower vehicle average selling price (ASP)” year-over-year, even after excluding currency effects. Automakers that can’t build cars fast enough usually raise prices, or at least stop discounting.

Tesla has more places to put battery cells than it used to. The same letter says energy storage had its “highest-ever order rate and backlog,” Megafactory Texas started production with 50 GWh of planned capacity, and Tesla is increasing 4680 cell output “to support the ramps of both Cybercab and Tesla Semi along with higher Model Y volumes.”

Tesla’s outlook even says deliveries depend on “allocation decisions between sale to customers and use for our owned and operated fleet.” So part of the battery constraint is Tesla deciding where its cells go.

Battery supply is a real issue, and tariffs on Chinese cells make it harder in the US. Tesla also did set records in a few markets, but overall deliveries are down, and Tesla is selling cars for lower than it used to. Those are not signs of a company that is supply constrained.

That is the excuses to spin. It doesn't matter what Musk says, his supporters will believe it.

In fact, today, in 2026, Tesla has more battery suppliers than ever, and it has itself ramped up production of its own battery cells.

But “we’re supply constrained” is one of Tesla’s oldest lines, and this letter doesn’t prove it. Deliveries fell year-over-year. Prices fell. Two quarters ago, Tesla built 50,000 cars it couldn’t sell. If batteries were really the bottleneck, Tesla would be raising prices and keeping the extra margin, not lowering ASPs.

The more likely answer is that it’s a bit of both. Demand recovered somewhat in some markets, and Tesla is choosing to send more cells to Megapack, Cybercab and Semi because it thinks those businesses are worth more. That’s a reasonable strategy. It’s just not the same as having more customers than it can serve.

#4974. Where Does Christine Baranski Live? Exploring the Gilded Age Star’s Real Estate Portfolio

Her Gilded Age character lives in a grand Upper East Side brownstone, but where does Christine Baranski live? The Emmy- and Tony–winning actor was born in Buffalo, New York, and still owns property in her home state in the form of a Manhattan pied-à-terre—and yes, like Agnes van Rhijn’s onscreen dwelling, it is on the Upper East Side. However, the Good Wife star primarily lives in Connecticut, where her late husband grew up and where the couple raised their two daughters, Isabel and Lily.

Read on to learn more about Baranski’s property portfolio.

For decades, Baranski has lived in Connecticut’s Litchfield County. Her first visit to the region was on a 1982 motorcycle ride; her future husband, fellow actor Matthew Cowles, was the driver. Cowles grew up in an 18th-century farmhouse in the small town of Bethlehem. “I had such a feeling of destiny about it,” Baranski recalled in a 2008 interview, “I loved it. I loved the smells in the air, the farms, the field. It was a dream. When Matthew took me into his home, I thought, ‘We’re gonna raise children here.’” The couple married the next year, briefly residing in an NYC apartment before returning to raise their daughters, born in 1984 and in 1987, in Cowles’s childhood home. “I had such a sense of eternity, like I was meant to be there,” she added.

A 2003 interview reported that Baranski primarily lived in Bethlehem and maintained a lake house about half an hour away, and it seems that this is still the case. “I have a marvelous house on a lake in Connecticut and I’ve hosted some very famous actors there,” the actor said in a recent interview with The Guardian, adding that those famed visitors have, on occasion, stripped naked for a swim. “It has a very long dock that has been ‘grandfathered’ in, as in they don’t allow a dock that long to be built anymore, but this is about 100 years old. You sit in the living room in summer and watch the sun set, and then go out into the evening and skinny dip in the lake.”

Cowles died in 2014, but Baranski remains deeply rooted in his hometown. The Mamma Mia! star is so entrenched in the community that she became active in the Housatonic Valley Association, a local environmental nonprofit, and currently serves as one of its directors. “I enjoy so much the beauty of Litchfield County,” Baranski said in 2009. “I couldn't imagine living in a more beautiful place.”

In 2004, Baranski bought a pied-à-terre on Manhattan’s Upper East Side for $1.27 million. Located in a 1920s structure where Jackie Kennedy lived as a child, the two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment featured a 21-foot-long living room with hardwood floors, a wood-burning fireplace flanked by built-in bookshelves, and yellow-striped wallpaper. A galley kitchen opened to a small dining room painted a soft sage green and decorated with elegant paintings in ornate gold frames, while the bedrooms were done up in distinct palettes: one was blue and white, while the other was tan with pops of red and orange. Both had their own en suite bath.

“Happily, now after years of commuting to LA and trying to do the whole bicoastal thing, The Good Wife shoots in Greenpoint, Brooklyn,” Baranski said in a 2011 New York Times article. “Our kids are grown up and in graduate school, so I have this life where I can enjoy the city and not worry about racing home to Connecticut.” The actor shared her typical Sunday routine in the city, which included reading in a café, visiting museums, and seeing friends. “I tend to call Sundays a girlfriend day because my husband is in Connecticut, so more often than not I’m alone here, which is a chance to catch up with girlfriends,” she said. “I might do a lunch at one of the hole-in-the-wall French bistros in the neighborhood, but sometimes I skip lunch in favor of an early dinner.” Then, the actor turns in early. “If I’m in town on a Sunday, it usually means I’m working Monday, and often I’m the first shot of the day, which means you’re up at 4:30. That means going to bed early. So I’ll go to my early dinner and then try to get myself to sleep by 9 or 9:30.”

Inhabitants of the co-op building, designed by architect Lafayette A. Goldstone, have access to a backyard garden, a gym, and a laundry room. Baranski listed her unit in the nine-story building in February 2021 for $1.39 million, and it sold that June.

Baranski didn’t move too far, however. In December 2020, the Good Fight star upgraded to a larger $2.2 million duplex unit in the same building. Listing photos showed that the home was sold with a few spaces under construction, so she likely added some custom touches before moving in. The apartment has four bedrooms, three bathrooms, and a much larger eat-in kitchen than the one found in Baranski’s previous unit. It still boasts a wood-burning fireplace in the living room, accessed from the foyer through an arched doorway. On its other end, the living room opens to a spacious formal dining room. A guest bedroom rounds out the lower level. The remaining bedrooms are at the top of a winding staircase. Another fireplace, tucked between built-ins, graces one bedroom, which shares a Jack-and-Jill bathroom with another bedroom—which could be used as a dressing room—that boasts six closets. The final bedroom has a full en suite bathroom.

#4970. How to Lose Fat and Build Muscle Sustainably as a Busy Mom—Your Realistic 4-Step Plan

A strength coach for moms outlines the key strength training and diet habits to adopt for lasting change.

For many moms returning to exercise after pregnancy, losing fat while building muscle can feel like a daunting goal.

“The odds are good that you lost some muscle mass during pregnancy. Maybe you weren’t training as much as you normally did or you weren’t training at all,” says Bailey, coach and founder of Well Mamas Coaching, in a recent YouTube video.

However, body recomposition is a gradual process, she explains, and consistency—“sticking with it”—matters far more than getting everything right.

“It's not [about] doing it perfectly. It's not having an hour to yourself every single day to do all this magical meal prep and green juicing,” she says.

“It's just jumping back in when you can and not buying into the start-stop cycle of...start[ing] over on Monday and find[ing] a new plan.”

Strength training with progressive overload is a “gold standard” pillar of a realistic body recomposition plan, Bailey says.

Progressive overload means gradually making your workouts more challenging over time by increasing the weight, number of repetitions, or training frequency, or by reducing your rest periods.

“This type of strength training is what signals your body...to adapt, change, and rebuild the muscle fibers that we're tearing down during these workouts, which is what helps you build muscle,” Bailey explains.

She recommends focusing on compound exercises such as squats, lunges, deadlifts, hip thrusts, and the bench press because “you're recruiting multiple muscle groups.”

As for your workout schedule, she reassures viewers that you don't need to train “six times a week...for 45 to 60 minutes.”

“Four workouts a week, 30 minutes or less, with progressive overload and compound moves...is plenty,” she says.

By now, it's well established that muscle growth and repair depend on eating enough protein.

“If you're not eating enough protein to repair the tears that you create in your muscles when you work out, then your body doesn't have the amino acids it needs to build those muscle fibers,” Bailey says.

She recommends aiming for around 30g of protein per meal. That's broadly in line with research showing that consuming around 25-30g of protein per meal is associated with greater lean mass and both upper- and lower-body strength in healthy women.

Good options include lean meat, beans, and legumes, yogurt, cottage cheese, and canned tuna.

“Mild” is the key word, Bailey emphasizes.

A calorie deficit means consuming fewer calories than your body burns each day.

“Of course, you do need to be in some sort of caloric deficit in order for fat loss to occur,” she reminds viewers.

However, the size of that deficit matters.

She recommends a moderate deficit of around 200-400 calories below your maintenance intake.

“That's just enough to prompt your body to use stored fat for energy,” she explains. “However, it's not so much that your body starts cannibalizing muscle.”

Research supports the importance of avoiding an overly aggressive calorie deficit, with one study finding that eating more than 500 fewer calories than required impaired gains in lean mass.

She adds one caveat for breastfeeding moms.

“You want to go above what I would calculate if you weren't nursing—anywhere from 400-800 additional calories per day,” she says.

Bailey acknowledges this can be difficult for moms.

“Often sleep and stress feel like they're not within our control,” she says.

However, sleep is essential because it's during recovery that muscle adapts and grows.

“The muscle...broken down through resistance training...is rebuilt...during sleep, while we're recovering,” she explains.

She also references research showing that sleep duration influences body recomposition, with shorter sleep associated with less fat loss.

If “a solid eight hours” isn't realistic, she suggests finding even a few extra minutes by cutting back on doomscrolling or late-night TV.

She also notes that chronically elevated cortisol levels associated with stress may interfere with muscle-building processes, recommending outdoor walks, deep breathing, or even guided meditation in the shower to create small moments of calm.

#4969. Tesla FSD ‘subscriptions’ hit 1.74M, counted the way Musk’s pay package wants

Tesla says it now has 1.74 million active “Full Self-Driving” subscriptions, up 67% from a year ago. A footnote in its Q3 2026 shareholder letter explains how it gets there: the metric follows “our 2025 CEO Performance Award” and “includes both upfront payment and monthly subscriptions.”

Here’s what Tesla has reported under that definition:

Tesla stopped selling FSD as a one-time purchase on February 14, 2026. New customers can only get it as a subscription, at $99 a month in the US. But everyone who paid upfront before that, at prices that reached $15,000, stays in the count as long as the car is active. The only exclusion is free trials.

We flagged this in April when Tesla reported 1.28 million. Six months later, Tesla still doesn’t say how many of the 1.74 million actually pay every month.

The same approach shows up elsewhere in the letter. Tesla’s “cumulative deliveries” figure, now 10.2 million, also counts “any unsupervised Robotaxis placed into commercial operation,” again to match the pay package, which has a 20 million vehicle milestone.

Tesla also says more than 75% of new deliveries in North America included FSD subscriptions in Q3, “a nearly twenty percentage point sequential increase.” It says it believes “FSD is driving demand in markets where it is available.”

That’s a big number, and Tesla doesn’t define it. The letter doesn’t say whether it counts subscriptions started at delivery with an introductory offer, or how many of those buyers are still paying after a few months. The active-subscription metric excludes free trials, but Tesla doesn’t say the same about the attach rate.

Musk’s 2025 award has 12 tranches. Each requires a market cap milestone and one operational milestone. The operational list includes 20 million vehicles delivered, 10 million active FSD subscriptions, 1 million Optimus robots, 1 million robotaxis in commercial operation, and adjusted EBITDA targets. As of June 30, Tesla considered only one of them probable: 20 million deliveries.

Tesla added 260,000 net FSD subscriptions in Q3, its best quarter yet. At that pace, it would take about eight years to reach 10 million. At the pace of the last 12 months, about 700,000 a year, it would take closer to 12. The award runs until 2035.

Counting people who bought FSD outright isn’t wrong on its own. Those cars do have the software. The problem is calling them “subscriptions” and presenting the total as proof of momentum, when the definition was written for Musk’s pay package and not for investors trying to understand the business.

The metrics that are far off in Musk's 2025 comp plan don't matter because if there is a change of control (i.e., SpaceX buys Tesla), all the comp plan metrics vest and count as achieved, and good old Elon gets paid. And you wonder why he wants this merger?

This is now Tesla’s headline software metric. The board wrote the definition, Musk’s compensation depends on it, and the company won’t say how many people pay $99 a month. Tesla obviously knows that number.

The attach rate is the more interesting claim, if it holds up. A 75% take rate on a $99-a-month product would be a real business. So show us the retention: how many North American buyers who started a subscription in Q2 are still paying today?

#4968. Even As a Wicker Man, Alexander Skarsgård’s Got Game. This Scent Will Give You Some Too.

The actor is the face of Valentino’s newest fragrance, Vendetta.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IF ANYONE CAN MAKE RATTAN hot, it’s Alexander Skarsgård. The actor’s latest film project, about a craftsman who creates a wicker husband (Skarsgård) for a lonely woman (played by Olivia Colman), has been an unlikely hit since its release in theaters last week. But basket weave isn’t the only material Skarsgård’s rocking—he’s been killing it on the red carpet lately, too.

There was the gold Saint Laurent suit earlier this month at the BFI London Film Festival, the sick Chopova Lowena skirt to promote Wicker at the Los Angeles premiere last week, and the head-to-toe Valentino outfit he wore at the house’s show during Paris Fashion Week. It seems there’s nothing Alexander Skarsgård can’t infuse with his unique brand of Swedish swag.

Shop the new Valentino Vendetta fragrance.

So, it should come as no surprise when Valentino tapped the 50-year-old star as one of the faces of its brand-new fragrance pillar, Vendetta (alongside Dakota Johnson for the women’s version). Unlike Valentino’s most famous scent family, Born in Roma, which features a spiked pyramid design, Vendetta’s bottle pays homage to the brand’s classic V motif, with a rich, sensual juice created by master perfumer Marie Salamagne.

You’ll get the sensuality from the campaign imagery, photographed by iconic duo Inez & Vinoodh, and the epic accompanying video, directed by French filmmaker Romain Gavras, but what about the fragrance itself?

“It has a boldness and a kind of self-assertive quality to it,” Skarsgård tells me when I ask him to describe the scent. “It’s not quite as heavy as I thought it would be. That first note of ginger has a lightness to it and then it evolves into those richer, deeper notes that last longer.”

For his part, Skarsgård says he’s a signature scent kind of guy—a far cry from the scentmaxxing approach of today’s TikTokers, who douse themselves in enough cologne to create their own noxious atmosphere.

“I’m a proponent of finding your fragrance and sticking with it,” he says. “You become associated with that smell, it becomes part of who you are.”

That’s not to say he hasn’t had his share of missteps. Born in Stockholm, Skarsgård began acting at a young age—his first film role came when he was just seven—but quit as a teenager to join the Swedish navy and, eventually, attend university. Along the way, he learned some valuable fragrance lessons, as most guys do. “I think when I was a teenager, I overdid it a lot,” he says. “You want to marry your scents, so it’s a combination of the fragrance and your own natural scent.”

A woody-spicy addition to the Valentino fragrance family, Vendetta is the first new scent pillar from the brand since its blockbuster Born in Roma.

It’s quite an evolution for a lad who equates childhood with the unmistakable aroma of sausage. When I ask Skarsgård about his first connection to fragrance—that unmistakably transformative power of scent—it’s the sausage factory that faced his front door.

“To this day, it really brings me back, and they’re fond memories,” he says. “Whenever I smell sausage, I’m an eight-year-old again. I’m getting ready for school, seeing my buddies, thinking about this girl I had a crush on. It strikes a chord.”

Of course, processed meat isn’t a key part of the olfactive experience of Vendetta Uomo. It opens with a sharp note of sparkling ginger with the typical brightness of a top note. From there, a warm, rich cinnamon liquor accord envelops the nose and gives way to earthy, grounding patchouli and woods. It’s at turns inviting and accessible while still drawing you in with something seductive and unique.

It’s sex in a spritz, the idea being that you too can have the appeal of a 6'4" Norse god. Ironically, Skarsgård’s everyday life couldn’t be more different from what he says most people see when he’s walking the red carpet or strutting his stuff on screen.

“When I’m not working, I’m trying to spend as little time as possible thinking about [my skincare and sartorial choices],” he says. “It’s all about comfort. I’ve been on a shoot for four months and I’ve been wearing the same shorts and flip-flops for months.”

But isn’t that part of the appeal of a fragrance—the ability to be a different person, someone out of your ordinary? Sure, you could be wearing a pair of sweats and a hat, but with a spray of Vendetta, you’re suddenly wearing a leopard-print overcoat on top of it.

It’s a good look. Just ask Alexander Skarsgård.

Shop the new Valentino Vendetta fragrance.

#4966. 10 Best Bedside Lamps & Table Lamps (2026)

Before you spin into a redecorating frenzy (step away from the chandeliers…), consider the transformative power of the table lamp. The best bedside lamps are a necessary lighting addition to any bedroom—nighttime reader or not. They also have staying power away from the bedside, should they find their home in another part of the house as your taste shifts: add them to a shelf on a bookcase, show them off in an entryway, let one adorn your kitchen countertop.

Accent lighting has always been a thing, but lately, with the rise of anti–Big Light content on TikTok and Reels, the demand for cute, trendy ambient lighting options is going way up. And we get it—relying on built-in overhead light fixtures feels cold and corporate, while smaller lamps create a warmer ambience. That’s why we had the bright idea to test a curated selection of top picks from some of our favorite brands (in addition to other great options that score high design marks in our books). In each of our reviews you’ll find an AD editor’s testimony as to what makes each light stand out, how they use it in their space, and what’s something buyers should keep in mind. The hardest part now will be deciding on just one (or two).

(Lamps pictured with a 2.4-ounce candle for size comparison)

The head is magnetized, so you can direct light in pretty much any direction you choose.

Flos’s Bilboquet Table Lamp, designed by Philippe Malouin, is another seen-before decor moment, as we tapped it for our 2025 gifting shoot. It’s been a mainstay at Fletcher’s work station ever since. “This sexy little lamp has a great glow and looks just as handsome when it isn't turned on,” she told us. “I keep it at my desk and it's a lovely distraction from the standard issue fluorescents here at 1WTC. I love that the bulbous chrome joint is a functional swivel point, which means it can spotlight almost 360 degrees.” An eco-friendly design as well, Flos crafted the lamp’s body from a byproduct of paper production and refrained from using any glue, so the components will be recyclable after a long life spent spotlighting your home.

A built-in dimmer switch allows you to customize the glow.

The switch requires a substantial turn to activate and may not be the best choice for illuminating a full workspace. If the Raffia Wave shade isn’t your style, there’s three other shade options available, along with a range of colored bases.

Looking for some living room table lighting with a touch of coastal grandma style? Look no further than this rattan lamp from Serena and Lily. With its petite size, the light can fill up empty nooks and crannies while perfectly illuminating them. “What immediately caught my eye was how the unique, trendy raffia shade complements the sleek ceramic base beautifully,” associate visuals editor Shani Kravetz told us. “The lamp is the perfect size for a desk or kitchen counter, adding a warm, ambient glow and delightful pop of style.”

A button controls this lamp's four-step dimmer.

If you're looking for a super bright desk or task lamp, this is not it! I'd also opt for a non matte option in the future because the black shows all the imperfections which, because I tote it around a lot, there are many bumps and bruises.

If you have an outdoor space, you know the importance of having a cordless lamp you can tote on the short journey inside to grab more drinks or snacks once the sun has gone down. Or maybe you want to guide guests to the backyard for a little midnight gossip session around the fire pit. Whatever it is, this rechargeable lamp is easy to grab and is available in a plethora of colors. With a “vaguely mushroomy” look according to Rachel, its small stature and four dimmable light levels makes it endlessly versatile. “I've seen them featured in Hypebeast homes, minimalist Barcelona bedrooms, tiny Sydney apartments, and grand Austin estates, so chances are it'll work for whatever design scheme resonates with you,” says Rachel. “The last note I'd make is that the price point is quite steep at over $300 for such a tiny piece. While there are lots of dupes on the market, I'd definitely stick with the original as it's been through the ringer with me for the last two years.”

This lamp comes in three different sizes. We tested the 9" version.

While it’s definitely not dim, this lamp might be best served as a mood lighting moment rather than a solid light source you’d want for reading or working.

This design-forward white table lamp (which is inspired by a Japanese lantern) has us doing a double take thanks to its silhouette and subtle texture. According to shopping editor Audrey Lee, “There’s something about this little lamp that’s incredibly soothing.” With a glass shape that doesn’t scream “light fixture,” it’s the perfect way to add pizzazz to any nightstand or dimly lit corner, especially if you prefer contemporary or postmodern design aesthetics. “This West Elm light emits a subtle glow in such a beautiful way, and I love that the ribbed design doesn’t disappear when it’s turned on,” says Audrey. “I like to have just this on if I’m about to turn in for the night but want to watch a show or two to help lull me to sleep—it’s just perfect.”

The adjustable top on this geometric lamp allows you to direct the light wherever you need it.

If you plan to place a lamp several feet from the nearest outlet, look no further; the Analog has a looooong cord. While I love that kind of flexibility, the excess is a bit bulky and difficult to tuck away neatly. It’s not a deal breaker by any means, but cable-management-heads may want to invest in some extra large cord clips to keep everything tidy.

Consider the Gantri Analog Task Lamp two-faced: It can set a mood and get down to work when it needs to. If there ever was a lamp that looked like it was going to sprout legs and march right off the table, this is it. There are three colors to choose from (stone, carbon, and persimmon), and the light switch has dimming capabilities. Visuals editor Lizzie Soufleris describes the piece as “a perfect desk lamp,” thanks to the dimmable light that can rotate a full 230 degrees in either direction. “Don’t let the oversized Rubik’s cube–esque look fool you–this lamp is highly functional,” she adds. “Plus, the exterior is made of GPP, Gantri’s sustainably sourced sugarcane polymer blend.”

Sheds more of an ambient glow rather than the direct light a task lamp might provide.

Perhaps Verner Panton’s most iconic lighting innovation, the Panthella lamp toys with scale, and continues to remain relevant with the modern design crowd. Available in both enlarged and shrunken versions of the original 1971 silhouettes, Fletcher calls this iconic design (known to pop up in many a home tour) one of the “quintessential ‘70s space age silhouettes…when Louis Poulsen released the mini, portable version in late 2024, I was all too happy to give it a spin.” The built-in LED sheds a warm white light with a dimmer that you can adjust by tapping the chrome topper.

Harrison warns that the lamp’s more casual silhouette might not be complementary to sophisticated setups. She also notes that the lamp requires a tedious amount of battery charging time—up to seven hours.

There’s a great chance you’ve crossed paths with a Zafferano Poldina lamp at some point—most likely sitting al fresco at a trendy bistro or stylish garden patio. Small but mighty, the Poldina lamp suits functionality more than expressive design without making an eyesore of itself. The lamp is suitable for indoors or outdoors, and its slim stature allows it to slot into the tightest spacest—meaning more room on your bedside table for an attractive alarm clock, skincare, paperback, and other nighttime essentials. Shopping writer Julia Harrison has this rechargeable table lamp in a sage matte, and finds it to be perfect task lighting for a desk or a little mise en place work in the kitchen. “It blends shyly and seamlessly into all setups that require a little, but not too much, light,” she says.

This lamp is pricey, but think of it as functional art. In a perfectly dim room it emits the most ethereal glow.

Lee admits that most of her lighting inspiration comes from Quarters, the vibey design showroom and retail concept space by Felicia Hung and Nick Ozemba of In Common With. “Good fixtures are a given when your space is put together by lighting designers, and there’s no shortage of excellent lamps, sconces, and chandeliers at every corner,” says Lee. For her, In Common With’s Fazzo lamp shines a smidge brighter than the rest. Amber-hued glass looks as though it's been draped on the rounded head of a bulb, resulting in a wispy silhouette and a glowy presence even when switched off. “I’ve been fortunate enough to attend a number of functions at Quarters and I always leave with a little less storage on my phone but 100 new lamp photos,” says Lee.

Because of the opaque shade, this lamp casts a softer, more diffused light than clear or fabric shades.

Inspired by Italian modernism, the mushroom shape of Rejuvenation’s Roland table lamp is made entirely of glass. The petite frame is only 10 inches tall, and the lamp casts a soft glow, diffused by the opaque shade. Despite not being dimmable, this bestseller’s light is never hard or stark white. Use this lamp for ambiance in your living room or on your bedside table.

The geometric form is completely transparent, showcasing all of the internal wiring and the light bulb. McGregor says that it’s also a notably heavy fixture.

AD100 designer Jeremiah Brent drew inspiration from 1940s architecture for this hand-cast glass lamp, which you may recognize as an honoree from our 2025 Best in Show edit. Pewter accents and subtle texture bring a contemporary elegance to the organic materials, giving the fixture inherent Brutalist appeal that swayed shopping market editor Kate McGregor. “This piece casts the ideal warm glow across my entire work surface. Solid and weighty, it’s the kind of lamp that will blend seamlessly with my decor evolution, whether it leans more eclectic one day, and more mod the next,” she says. McGregor notes that the design’s transparency translates to a visible lightbulb “which, with my current standard bulb, I’m not sure how I feel about, but with an eddison or big globe option, it becomes a statement,” she says.

Interiors guru Shea McGee brings her penchant for reimagining classic design with this coastal table lamp. While its bulbous base draws your eye, the sloping shade gives it a more traditional silhouette. Wrapping the entire design in wicker brings a contemporary twist, reminiscent of our new favorite movie. This fixture is a versatile choice—we picture it accenting more reserved interiors or eclectic design schemes , especially in the ‘chive’ green hue.

Bulb type: 60 watt max; 9 watt LED max recommended

The Lulu & Georgia Camas Table Lamp is a masterclass in mixing materials. Grounded by a no-frills brass base, the dramatically ruched linen shade is the main force driving this lamp’s design. Ribbons on each side of the shade’s base layer in even more texture and charm, tying the piece together (pun intended).

Bulb type: A19 LED Filament Bulb, 9W recommended

Care for an infusion of rustic Italian farmhouse style? Heidi Caillier’s on the case. Decorative lug handles and a green glaze suggest heirloom. Your secret? There’s no Tuscan vineyard written into your inheritance, though this lamp might have your guests assuming otherwise.

Don’t sleep on IKEA’s newer collections. The spherical FADO lamp has taken over TikTok because of its versatility with a number of different interior design styles. Our favorite tip? Use a smart lightbulb to change the color (say, pink or orange) for a tasteful pop of whimsy in your home.

Anointed a reader favorite from our Best in Show lookback, this mixed material light from Istanbul-based designer Merve Kahraman embraces the checkerboard trend with a coastal edge. It’s available in two different sizes to accent bedside tables, credenzas, or consoles of all proportions, and supply a subtle amount of color in either green or red. It’s important to note that you need a particularly narrow bulb to fit in the rattan shade, as it doesn’t disassemble.

Bulb type: 60 watt max; 9 watt LED max recommended

We think traditionalists will gravitate towards this streamlined pick from AD100 firm Pierce & Ward. The design's flattened surfaces feel like a novel take on form, bringing just the right amount of dimension to your nightstands or desktops. The dandelion-hue linen shade offers just a hint of color, while the rounded ceramic base’s earthy finish feels like a natural fit in a minimalist’s space.

Bulb type: 60 watt max; 9 watt LED max recommended

“This delightful, kelly green lamp changes brightness levels with the touch of a button and charges in mere hours—it even goes outside,” muses McGregor. Rechargeable and portable, the Suki lamp from Kate Spade is minimal but bold, suiting a plethora of design styles from midcentury to space age and postmodern. “I’m a sucker for a portable lamp, and this one that actually has the power to illuminate my entire bedroom in an ambient glow,” says McGregor,

The best part of this Gantri table lamp is its 26 different color-blocking combos.“If I could, I’d have 12 of these lamps across my house, each with a different color base,” says shopping writer Julia Harrison. While her Lago sits atop a stack of books on her desk, it’s been known to move around her house to function as a reading light, a bedside table lamp, and task lighting for late-night puzzling. The Lagos sheds a warm white light perfect for winding down and doing a bit of reading (ie: scrolling) before lights out. The red base and white shade would look particularly cute bedside, especially next to a striped bedding setup.

While you can use a higher watt light bulb than your light fixture suggests, we wouldn’t recommend it. Wattage relates to how much power a particular device uses, and if more than the design allows is being used, you face the risk of ‘overlamping,’ meaning your fixture will start to run particularly hot. This is bad for a few reasons: Overheating can melt bulb sockets and wiring and, in the worst cases, lead to an electrical fire. It may also cost you more in the long run and be less energy-efficient—if your bulbs are drawing too much energy, it’ll likely mean having to replace them more frequently. If you’re still confused on the correct bulb to look for, we hope this handy visual guide will help.

There are many factors we considered for each of our reviews to give you the insight you need to select the best table lamps for your home, namely the following:

Brand snobs: While thousands of companies produce lighting, it’s hard to know who won’t try to sell you dollhouse-sized decor or a fixture with faulty wiring. That’s why we’ve used our brand expertise and design discernment to bring you options from labels you can trust (because we trust them enough to buy from them ourselves!). From brands like West Elm and Wayfair who also produce a sensational sectional or bookshelf to more indie names like Gantri, who specialize in the all things lighting.

Delivery and assembly: Did our package arrive within the guaranteed 10-day delivery window? Was the delicate porcelain base carefully packed with the necessary cushioning? Did the instruction manual for assembly look like it could have been ripped out of an astrophysics textbook? We wanted to let you know exactly what to expect from your purchases and called out anything surprising. We also double-checked if a brand provided you with a complimentary bulb or if it’s something you should add to your next Amazon order.

Sizing: While we provide specs on exact measurements in all these reviews, sizing can still be a difficult factor to gauge. To help you determine whether or not that CB2 lamp will totally overwhelm your nightstand as well as help you compare the lamps of this list, we shot each close-up with a 2.4-ounce candle as a base point for size comparison.

What makes this lamp unique? Does the lamp’s design fit a clear aesthetic? Does it function particularly well in a specific area of the house? Incredibly easy to use? Our reviews were designed to give insight on why each lamp could be the right lamp for your Scandi oasis or midcentury abode. We also wrote about any ingenious details that show how thoughtful the designer was as well as why the piece was just what our tester was looking for.

What to keep in mind: Nobody’s perfect, and beauty can be in the eye of the beholder—which is why each lamp also has a note detailing what a potential buyer should keep in mind. For example, if assembly was particularly difficult, the lamp is extremely delicate or hard to clean, and who the design might not be suited for.

#4965. 5 Reasons to Fall in Love with La Quinta

Whether you’re visiting to play, explore, or simply chill, this desert paradise in California’s Coachella Valley has a little something for everyone.

Every day, from deciding whether or not to hit snooze to choosing to read a few more pages before shutting our eyes, our brains are a blur of choices—approximately 35,000 according to prevailing research. And frankly, it’s exhausting trying to make the right one every time. A vacation reboot would help… but travel planning requires even more decisions, which obviously defeats the purpose. And so the trip gets backburnered again.

What if there was a place that made choosing easy—because there’s no possible wrong answer? A land where you could decide to do all the things on the visitor’s bureau checklist, or none of them, and have an equally good time?

Enter La Quinta, California, a city of championship golf courses, towering palms, sprawling resorts with pools and spas, Old Hollywood lore, dramatic mountain backdrops, purple skies at dusk, and savory restaurants tucked into a calm corner of the Coachella Valley. It’s a place where you’re encouraged to do only what you love and what makes you feel most alive. Here in this sun-kissed slice of paradise, choose to follow the itinerary that is most Quinta-ssentially you.

There are 20 golf courses within the city limits, including the nine at the PGA West, a 2,000-acre luxury golf resort and community. Among those are the Mountain Course and the Stadium Course, which blend stunning natural beauty, manicured landscapes, challenging holes and expert designs by masters Pete Dye, Jack Nicklaus, and Greg Norman.

You can hit up the pickleball and tennis courts at Fritz Burns Park from dawn until well past dusk. The 12-acre green space also features a skate park, a children’s playground, a pool, and a dedicated area to play fetch with your pup. If you need to brush up on the rules of your chosen game, book some time with the pros at La Quinta Resort & Club, where you can rent equipment or pick up a match.

Whether you’re craving laid-back brunch bites, like the huckleberry hotcakes or double smashburgers at the farm-to-table eatery Beautiful Day, or a night on the town enjoying minty lamb chops and mai tais exploding with citrusy pucker at DSRT Club, La Quinta’s culinary scene does not disappoint.

Greet the day with Mexican delicacies like machaca or chilaquiles on the colorful porch at Casa Mendoza. If you have a hankering for south-of-the-border specialties later in the day, they also make a mean molcajete, seafood enchiladas, or tacos al pastor. Come afternoon, head to La Quinta Cliffhouse for the legendary nightly happy hour and stay for supper at sunset. There, you can put the date in date night by snacking on Medjools with bacon, blue cheese, coconut, and honey. (Pro tip: always order the gooey stone fruit however it’s served, whether as a shake, syrup or side dish—the Coachella Valley grows 95% of the dates in the U.S.) Close out the night with a slice of decadent Toll House Pie, a fixture at The Sandbar for four decades.

Those who believe it is just as important to nourish the mind as it is the body can take a walk down memory lane at the free La Quinta Museum, where the newly expanded history and culture exhibit details the people, technologies, and businesses that shaped the city, including the Cahuilla Indians, homesteaders, the railroad, and the celebrity magnet La Quinta Resort, which is celebrating its centennial this year. At the museum, visual learners can study the massive mural and a collection of photographs.

La Quinta itself is a patron of the arts. It’s hard to miss the more than 160 sculptures, murals, and decorated utility boxes installed through the Art In Public Places program. Twice a year, creatives from around the world descend on the civic center campus and turn it into a concert venue and an alfresco art gallery for a four-day festival. After admiring the artwork, head over to Old Town for locally made mementos. The charming retail district—known for its pleasing Spanish colonial architecture and vibrant sprays of bougainvillea—stocks gems at independent boutiques and galleries year-round and hosts the open-air Art on Main Street event on select Saturdays from November to April.

The area is a bonanza for outdoor activity. Bike along the base of the Santa Rosa Mountains using the paved, 2.7-mile-long Bear Creek Trail, or fix your attitude by gaining altitude on the miles of trails littered throughout the Santa Rosa and San Jacinto mountain ranges.

One popular route takes hikers a little more than six miles from the La Quinta Cove neighborhood to Lake Cahuilla, which is particularly peaceful at dawn or dusk. (The luckiest trekkers spy bighorn sheep.) Go straight to the lake to picnic, go horseback riding, or fish. Prolong your city escape by pitching a tent and camping at Cahuilla. Sunrise yoga and movie screenings are also offered lakeside.

While it’s clear there’s lots to do, know that, in the LQ, doing nothing is always on the table. Downtime happens to be a desert specialty, as there’s always a cold pool, a chaise lounge, and an umbrella drink calling your name. In fact, La Quinta Resort & Club boasts 42 pools across the 45-acre property, including a family-friendly splash zone and a more serene adults-only plunge with private cabanas and movie nights. (Don’t forget the 53 hot tubs for crisp Coachella nights.) Those who enjoy night swimming should post up at the never-closed pool at The Chateau at Lake La Quinta.

Finish the evening with stargazing and a glass of something sparkling in front of the fire pits. To really lean into relaxation, melt into a hot stone massage at Coral Spa or happily drift off while indulging in chromotherapy, a steam bath, or a dreamy scalp rub at Spa La Quinta. Or tap into an even deeper state of zen by joining a meditation or breathwork session or Sound Bath Sundays at Gather Yoga in Old Town. Plan your easiest trip ever today.

#4963. Tesla energy revenue drops 16% as it refunds customers over tariffs

Tesla’s energy business deployed more batteries in Q3 2026 but brought in less money. Energy generation and storage revenue fell 16% year-over-year to $2.88 billion, even though storage deployments rose 10% to 13.7 GWh.

Tesla’s shareholder letter blames the drop “partially” on “tariff-related customer refunds.” It doesn’t say how much it refunded, to which customers, or why it was accounted for as reduced revenue.

Here’s how the segment has moved over the last five quarters, based on Tesla’s reported results:

Gross margin bounced back to 33.1% from 20.4% in Q2. But energy gross profit still fell to $954 million from $1.07 billion a year ago, and Tesla listed “lower Energy Generation and Storage gross profit” among the reasons its operating income fell 56%.

Year-to-date, Tesla has deployed 36 GWh, up 11% from 32.5 GWh over the same period of 2025. Energy revenue is down 6% to $8.43 billion. Deployments also came in well short of the roughly 15.9 GWh analysts expected for Q3.

This isn’t the first time tariffs have shown up in the energy segment this year. In Q1, Tesla listed “energy one-time benefits related to tariffs” among the drivers of its profit improvement, and energy gross margin hit 39.5%. We questioned those levers at the time, and Tesla never put a dollar figure on the energy portion.

Now money is flowing the other way. Tesla doesn’t explain the refunds, but the most likely reading is that some storage customers paid tariff-related charges that Tesla no longer owed after the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February. That’s a guess, though, and the letter leaves investors to make it.

The rest of the energy news in the letter is about getting tariffs out of the supply chain. Megafactory Texas started production with 50 GWh of planned capacity, alongside 40 GWh in California and 20 GWh in Shanghai. Tesla also shipped its first Megapacks built entirely with its own LFP cells from Nevada, where it has 7 GWh of cell capacity in early ramp.

Tesla says storage demand is at its “highest-ever order rate and backlog,” driven by data centers that need power faster than the grid can deliver it. One of those customers is Musk’s own: xAI, now part of SpaceX, bought another $269 million of Megapacks this year, after $430 million of purchases from Tesla in 2025.

Props to Tesla for refunding its customers on the same day that GM is enriching its board with corporate stock buybacks, to the tune of tens of billions.

Energy was supposed to be the steady part of Tesla while the car business stalled. This year it’s been anything but steady: a 39.5% margin in Q1, 20.4% in Q2, 33.1% in Q3, and revenue down even as deployments rise. A lot of that noise is tariffs, and Tesla keeps describing them without quantifying them.

Now, if Tesla is really reimbursing customers for tariffs, it’s a good thing. Many companies getting tariffs refund are pocketing them.So kudos to Tesla.

With that said, the company’s own CEO is responsible for getting elected the clown who installed those illegal tariffs in the first place. So…

#4961. Why Women Over 50 Should Add This Underrated Carry to Their Strength Routine

“Many people think core training means crunches or planks, but one of the most functional ways to strengthen the core is by learning to resist movement,” says personal trainer Alice Jordan.

Her go-to exercise for doing exactly that? The kettlebell suitcase carry.

“Holding a kettlebell in one hand and walking with good posture forces the deep abdominal muscles, obliques, and spinal stabilizers to work continuously to keep your body upright,” explains Jordan, who specializes in strength training during perimenopause.

“For women over 50, this is particularly valuable because it develops balance, posture and stability while also improving grip strength, which is an important marker of healthy aging,” notes Jordan.

Indeed, one landmark study published in The Lancet found that lower grip strength was consistently associated with a higher risk of early death—even after accounting for age, physical activity, smoking, body size, and other cardiovascular risk factors. Notably, the researchers reported that grip strength predicted somebody’s risk of dying better than systolic blood pressure.

The single-arm kettlebell suitcase carry, adds Jordan, “also translates directly into everyday activities such as carrying shopping, lifting luggage, or playing with grandchildren, making it a highly functional exercise.”

Below, Jordan explains how to do the exercise effectively and safely.

“Aim to include the exercise 2-3 times per week as part of a strength training program. It’s particularly effective when performed after your main strength exercises or as part of your core training,” adds Jordan.

As for how heavy a weight you should use for this exercise, Jordan recommends “choosing a kettlebell that feels challenging while still allowing you to maintain perfect posture throughout the walk.”

“You should be able to resist leaning to one side, keep your shoulders level and your core engaged from start to finish,” she adds.

“As a general guide, beginners might start with around 15-20 lb, while those with more strength training experience may use 20-30 lb or heavier, depending on their ability.”

Below, Jordan highlights four key mistakes to avoid while performing this exercise.

She especially enjoys interviewing those working within the community to improve access to sport, exercise and wellness. Hannah is a 2024 John Schofield Trust Fellow and was also named a 2022 Rising Star in Journalism by The Printing Charity.  A keen runner, Hannah was firmly a sprinter growing up (also dabbling in long jump) but has since transitioned to longer-distance running. #4959. Quince’s $190 Quilt Set Is Worth Every Dollar

Since its 2018 founding, Quince’s enormous catalog and affordable prices have captured national attention, leading many a shopper to wonder whether the brand was too good to be true. The shopping team at AD set out for an answer by putting Quince’s full lineup to the test. Ultimately, we found 17 favorite items.

The direct-to-consumer retailer’s bamboo sheets are among our favorite sets on the market, and its linen sheets get top marks for that bedding category. Quince’s curtains and towels, too, have made us fans, and its velvet sectional received high praise from our audience development manager.

Given the brand’s well-established pattern of creating buy-worthy textiles and furniture, I was excited to test its newest fall bedding collection. As a quilt connoisseur, I opted to start with the European Linen Cotton Stitch Quilt Set—with shams, obviously. In light of the thermostat-swinging nature of the fall weather, I hoped the quilt set could function as a trans-seasonal solution and give my room a noticeable (and needed) refresh.

Quilts are often heavy, so I was surprised by how lightweight the package felt before I even unboxed it. As it turns out, the quilt is light by design, constructed from a combination of linen and cotton, with cotton fill that weighs just 200 grams per square meter (gsm)—or about the same as a flannel shirt by the square meter. I was relieved by its lack of heft, as my New York apartment’s heat runs on radiators that I can’t control and is, as a result, basically blazing hot at all times. Upon situating the quilt on my bed, I immediately searched the pick-stitching for loose threads. Devastatingly, I found some—a few pulled threads around the border—though not so exaggerated that I’d need to make my bed with caution.

The quilt set is framed by jade lamps and maroon shades to give surrounding color.

My experience with this quilt set was, in a word, peaceful. The best quilts offer a little warmth, a little weight, and you can comfortably pull them up and over you without struggling or yanking. All of that is possible with this Quince style. I like sleeping totally wrapped in this quilt. Because of the aforementioned radiator situation, it would be unbearably hot if I tried pairing this with a comforter, so I had only a flat sheet between myself and the quilt, which I found to be the perfect pairing. Its low-loft, pick-stitch construction and weight made it extremely easy to create a crisp bedscape. Its texture also disguises sheet wrinkles and lies super flat without much effort at all. I especially appreciate this quality in the shams, since my pillows usually look wrinkled and misshapen. And I do recommend opting for the bundle with the shams, which keep things looking put together.

After the quilt had a spin through the laundry, I noticed no differences in its soft feel. It came out of the dryer wrinkle-free, without any hint of being frayed or fried. And that’s saying something, as I battle-tested this quilt in a New York laundromat where it endured high heat and no option for a gentle cycle.

At $190 for a total bed refresh, this high-quality set is a nice buy. I love how it lies, and I believe it’ll be a big win for anyone who hates making their bed. The quilt set makes the center of my room look polished, but not stuffy. It skews a bit casual for my maximal taste, but I love the warm ivory option for a great guest-room spread, where I keep things more uniform and less lavish. Ultimately, the weight, the feel, and the price point make it one of the most solid quilt-set choices I’ve come across in my very diligent searching.

#4958. It’s finally here: Porsche puts wireless charging into production [UPDATE]

Buried in a press release titled, “Even more colours and even greater convenience for the Cayenne Electric” was news that Porsche, for the first time, would be offering electrically wireless inductive charging on its impressively powerful Cayenne Electric SUV.

In a new explainer video released today, Porsche explains how its engineers developed inductive charging for the Cayenne Electric, from the transfer of power across an air gap to detecting foreign objects, guiding the car into position, and testing the system in real-world conditions without microwaving the family pet.

You can click the “play” button, at top, and read the original press release that came out a few weeks ago, below. Enjoy!

With the launch of Porsche Wireless Charging in its latest Cayenne Electric SUV, Porsche is introducing a particularly convenient form of EV charging that makes living with its most powerful car EVER even simpler than before: instead of connecting a cable, Cayenne drivers just have to park their portly P-car over a strategically placed pad, and the charging process then begins automatically.

The Porsche Wireless Charging system pairs a charging pad on the underside of the Cayenne with a ground pad installed in the customer’s parking space. Porsche calls the latter “weatherproof” for outdoor installation, and claims a charging rate of up to 11 kW and with an efficiency of about 90% for easy overnight charging.

Integrated safety mechanisms like motion sensors and cat foreign object detection are baked in to avoid microwaving the cat ensure safe operation, designed to stop the charging process automatically if, “a living creature comes close to the vehicle or the ground pad or if a metallic object lies on the latter and heats up.”

Porsche Wireless Charging is being rolled out globally in stages, and is available to order now in Germany and other European markets.

So this system was designed and engineered by a company in Germany and there is a Society of Automotive Engineers standard for both the pad and the receiver in the car. This could be showing up in other vehicles too.

If you’re not there, feel free to use wireless charging to your advantage and negotiate a crazy deal for yourself on a new Cayenne that’s on the lot today – or just watch the wireless charging explainer video, below, and let us know what you think of Porsche’s new plug-less plug-in in the comments section at the bottom of the page.

This TikTok-famous sneaker reigns supreme for walking and has earned a spot in our guides to the best platform sneakers and best travel shoes for good reason: it delivers all-day comfort without looking overly athletic. Plantar fasciitis and the heel pain that comes with it can quickly halt your walking workouts. The 2025 WH Fitness Award-winning, best overall plantar fasciitis walking shoe, Brooks Women’s Adrenaline GTS 24, delivers stability and support to keep you (and your plantar fascia) feeling good over time.

The New Balance 608 V5 Trainer has over 38,000 Amazon reviews, and for good reason. The brand integrated its signature ABZORB midsole, designed to reduce joint impact during walking through its cushioning and compression resistance. Plus, they come in narrow, standard, and wide sizing.

#4953. 7 Best Throw Blanket Picks for Cozy Nights, Tested by AD (2026)

With cool evenings underway, and a list of books to keep me sane throughout winter, I’ve done my due diligence of putting together a comprehensive throw blanket list for a cozy night in. I’ve rounded up my personal favorites and asked other Shop AD writers which ones they love for movie marathons, napping, and working from home.

Our top picks are made from quality materials like Grade-A Mongolian cashmere and merino wool that are smooth and soft without feeling too heavy for lounging. The design factor was just as important in our research. As much as I love a neutral blanket that can blend in any background, these blankets come in a range of colors and patterns to fit different interior styles—some even created by design icons like Alexander Girard. I’ve prioritized machine-washable options, with a couple of worthy exceptions, and included care instructions so you know what to expect on laundry day. Browse all of the best blankets below.

This throw’s “Matisse” name is fitting because it’s a true masterpiece. The wool-blend blanket has made the rounds across the Shop AD team’s desks all year since it’s just as vibrant as it is thoughtfully made. It’s designed by Ezcaray, a Spain-based, family-owned and -operated textile house, known for artisan-made pieces like this one that are hand-washed, -dyed, and -woven. I had it for a while at my desk and can confirm that the “prairie sunrise” blanket’s colors look rich like pictured online. I wouldn’t consider myself a maximalist by any means, but I do appreciate the “more is more” color combinations and how easy it would be to style this in an eclectic bedroom filled with collected decor. In terms of texture, I’d say it almost feels like a goldendoodle’s fur. The fabric is soft like you’d expect, but it almost has a silkiness to it, likely because of the mohair added in the blend. The best part is that it has held up beautifully all year long with no signs of shedding.

If you want a blanket that’s soft without feeling weighty, you can’t go wrong with a good cashmere throw. I always look out for Grade-A Mongolian cashmere in particular since its fine, long fibers are more durable than cheaper cashmeres, like Grade-C, or wool blends. My colleague Lauren Arzbaecher, Shop AD shopping producer, put Quince’s version on my radar last year after talking about it so enthusiastically at the office. She told me it felt “insanely soft” and always kept her comfortably “bundled up while reading a good book.”

My take? Everything Arzbaecher told me was true plus more. It feels breathable enough to keep me warm without sweating on the nights my apartment radiator is cranked up too high. I have the blanket in a deep moss color that fits my moody home design, but there are a dozen other colors, so you can find what works best for your space.

Even though I’ve tried my fair share of soft throw blankets in my life, this one is a favorite since it hits a trifecta of sorts: It’s incredibly fluffy, warm, and easy to care for. It’s made of 100% faux mohair, but Pom Pom at Home has me fooled. The blanket has a brushed finish that gives the blanket an ultrasoft feel, so much so that it’s quickly become my cold-weather companion this year. Ever since the temperature dipped below 50 degrees, I’ve kept it draped on my sofa for countless naps and cozy movie nights.

Fair warning: I’m quite gentle with this blanket, but I could see it easily snagging on sharp furniture corners if you’re not mindful. I haven’t noticed general material shedding in the last couple of months I’ve had the blanket, so that’s a good sign for longevity, especially since it’s a fuzzier-looking fabric.

Of course, I’d prefer it if it were made of pure mohair, but the fact that it resembles the material without looking or feeling cheap is a huge win. I’d recommend this piece to anyone who wants a plushy blanket without paying a steep price.

Architect and interior designer Alexander Girard wore a few hats during his career, one of them being a textile designer for Braniff International Airways. He designed this blanket as part of a 17,543-item brand-identity system for the airline, known for its bold design, in 1965. Today, Pendleton re-creates the iconic multi-stripe design, and we think it’s a great choice for anyone looking for a personality piece. “As a design enthusiast, no surface of mine goes unadorned—even a lowly desk chair deserves a decorative blanket, especially in a chilly office like Condé Nast’s with the AC blasting,” says Arzbaecher. “This striped wool throw rests over the back of my office chair, providing extra cushion and much-needed color.”

The design is understandably a huge draw, but its texture deserves just as much attention. It’s a smooth wool blend (82% wool and 18% cotton), and Arzbaecher does not find it the least bit “scratchy or too thick to the touch.”

Contributor Yelena Alpert considers this her travel blanket—it moves from her bed to the family room couch, and everyone fights over who gets to curl up under it. “The grand waffle texture is certainly noteworthy, but it is the warmth factor that makes this throw a winner,” she says, adding that it feels like her favorite cable-knit sweater. “Since it is made from merino wool, your body is immediately ensconced as if in a hug. It does not feel scratchy or itchy, in case you have a fear of wool.” The knotted fringe at the end of the throw might seem like a minimal detail, but Alpert says it makes her sectional look even cozier to snuggle up on.

“I am also a huge fan of the camel color,” she says. “It pairs so beautifully with my plum matelassé duvet cover, but also enriches the rosewood hue of my velvet quilt.”

My pretty-in-pink throw blanket has never failed to put a smile on my face in the last year. Its salmon color is vibrant and warm without going full Barbiecore. It’s also the most detailed herringbone blanket I’ve ever had—for those who are new to this design too, the pattern has a distinct V shape that looks like the skeleton of a herring fish. Sadly, some of the little loops have snagged on my watch as I’ve unwrapped myself to get up for a lunch break, so it’s something to think about if you’re worried about a pet clawing at your blanket.

The throw is another mainstay at my office desk when I need to thaw out after a cold subway commute, and it hasn’t disappointed. I’ve even lent it to my coworkers who could use an extra layer during the day, and they say it’s warm without feeling stuffy.

This is technically a bed blanket, so the size ranges from a Twin to a California King, but it doesn’t have the typical bulk of a big bedspread. Alpert likes the blanket since it’s lightweight and folds pretty flat when she places it at the foot of her bed. “I love the barely-there feel of the blanket and use it almost every night as I read stories to my son,” she says. “It provides just enough cover to keep me comfortable without putting me to sleep.” It also features thoughtful, grid-like stitching that gives her whole sleep setup a little extra character.

In true Brooklinen fashion, there are a few distinct hues to choose from, including muted and vibrant colors. “I have this in the storm [colorway], a somewhat dusty blue—and as the name would suggest, it looks like the sky before it rains,” Alpert says. “It almost works like a neutral and pairs well against a crisp white sheet—I use it with a percale cotton set, which has swirls of blue. I also use it with my linen sheets, and it creates this decadent, heirloom-quality bed.”
